new_statements.quote: [p.82] An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly. In Asilulu this is not the case. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root word; additions of suffixes do not affect this stress. [...] This obligatory penultimate stress rule not only sometimes obscures cognate reflexes but in a few cases seems to be the motivating force for certain vowel deletions in the antepenultimate syllable. All Hoamoal languages agree in vowel deletion in at least two lexical items. [p.62, Map 7 legend] d-e-k-l-m West Hoamoal; d-e Proto-Manipa; d Batumerah; e Manipa

new_statements.rule_in_words: In all Hoamoal languages (Collins's West Piru Bay subgroup comprising Manipa, Batumerah, Kelang, Luhu/Piru, Boano and Wakasihu/Allang/Larike), stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the whole phonological word, counting suffixes and enclitic particles, so stress moves rightward whenever a suffix or particle is added; this contrasts with Asilulu, where stress stays on the penult of the root.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Collins notes that the rule interacts with the many obligatory suffixes/postparticles of Hoamoal languages (Manipa pronouns a?une, anene, ine, amine, cene, imine, reli carry petrified demonstratives) and drives antepenultimate vowel deletion in a few items (Manipa ?alulana 'wave', sume?e 'shove', mannai 'male').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on the phonological word including suffixes and cliticised particles, based on Collins's own 1977-79 fieldnotes (he cites 'more than two thousand words' of Manipa material, p.77). The rule is stated for the Hoamoal subgroup as a whole and illustrated with Luhu vs Asilulu citation forms; Manipa forms are given in the same tables but without stress diacritics, so no Manipa word is shown with its stress marked.
new_statements.identity_note: Manipa [mqp], mani1297, is the sole language of Manipa Island (Ethnologue dialects Masawoy, Tomalehu, Tuniwara; OLAC alt. name Soow Huhelia). Collins 1983 groups Manipa with Batumerah as 'Proto-Manipa' inside West Hoamoal (with Kelang, Luhu, Piru); East Hoamoal = Boano, Wakasihu, Allang, Larike. The quoted stress rule is stated for the whole Hoamoal branch and exemplified with Luhu (luhu1243) vs Asilulu; Manipa forms appear in the same tables without stress marks. No language-specific description of Manipa exists in Glottolog, OLAC, Crossref, DOAJ or Semantic Scholar.

sources.note: p.82 (PDF p.92): 'An important phonological rule distinguishes all Hoamoal languages from Asilulu. Stress in Hoamoal languages is always penultimate; if a suffix or particle is added to the word the stress shifts accordingly' (contrasted with Asilulu root-penult stress; examples with stress marks are Asilulu and Luhu only, e.g. Luhu hulane, ulule, rawa?e, [pala?e?ena]).
